results.description:
This poster (or placard) was found in the grounds of Sandringham School after protests against the last rugby test of the Springbok rugby tour on 12 September 1981 in Auckland. That day, clashes between protesters, tour supporters and the police, became particularly violent as can be seen in the dirty, crumpled state of this poster.
The Springbok Rugby Tour of 1981 was a seminal event in New Zealand's political and social history - exposing deep rifts in society. Many New Zealanders objected to the tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid, and many questioned racism at home. Protests caused obstruction and the cancellation of games, and violence escalated between protesters, supporters and police during the tour.

creator: Wellington Media Collective
David Kent
Kathy Baxter
Chris McBride
results.description:
This poster was created for protests against the 1981 tour of New Zealand by the South African Springbok rugby team. Many New Zealanders objected to the tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid.
The poster called for a nationwide mobilisation on 3 July 1981 in an effort to force the New Zealand government to reconsider the tour. The poster features a crowd of protesters carrying a banner seen at the earlier mobilisation on 1 May 1981. The image of a protesting crowd is important to protest propaganda as it shows solidarity with a cause and leaves a 'quotable' visual record, which can be easily repurposed for subsequent protest material.
Thousands of people marched throughout the country on both mobilisations. The tour went ahead (with the first game playing in Gisborne on 22 July), but protest action continued throughout, sometimes resulting in violence between protesters, supporters and police, eventually forcing the cancellation of two games.
Wellington Media Collective
The poster was designed and printed by Kathy Baxter, Dave Kent and Chris McBride of Wellington Media Collective. WMC was established in November 1978. Its mission statement 'We will work with you, not for you' enabled communities and activists to create advertising and protest material with the support of professional designers.

results.description: This poster was created and printed very quickly by artist David Blair in response to renewed police efforts to evict Ngāti Whātua protestors from their land at Bastion Point / Takaparahwau. Police had surrounded the protestors and chanted 'Move move move' as they had during the Springbok rugby tour protests the year before in 1981. Protesters had driven some cows from a nearby paddock into police lines.Blair printed about 100 copies and gave them to Joe Hawke and the protestors, who stuck them on the barbed wire fence facing the police. The humour of the posters helped diffuse the situation.Blair was part of Auckland Artists Action which was founded during the Springbok tour in 1981.

creator: Coalition Against Nuclear Warships
results.description:
This poster protested against the visit of the USS Texas to Wellington on 10 August 1983. Over 10,000 people marched in a lunch-time protest during the ship's visit, including School Children Against the Texas (SCAT). Posters and slogans were plastered up throughout the city.
The poster was created by the Coalition Against Nuclear Warships (CANWAR, founded in 1976) which was a coalition of peace groups opposed to nuclear-armed or powered ships visiting New Zealand ports. For example, Wellington received five such visits between 1976 and 1984: USS Truxton in August 1976, September 1980 and May 1982; the USS Texas in August 1983; and the HMS Invincible in August 1984. As in other ports, each visit was met with protests in the city and on the harbour, with the Peace Squadron confronting the vessels.

results.description: This poster advertised a poster exhibition calling for artists to contribute 50 prints of topical posters to raise money for a campaign to stop the New Zealand Rugby Union's proposed tour of South Africa in 1985.The exhibition was held in Auckland and supported by the National Council of Churches. Peter Lange came up with name, JustArt. About twenty artists were involved, and many were connected to Artists Against Apartheid (which had become Auckland Artists Action by this time).This was only four years after the bruising experience of the Springbok rugby tour to New Zealand in 1981. Many New Zealanders had objected to that tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid. Protests had caused obstruction and the cancellation of games, and much violence between protesters, supporters and police.The posters were activist in intent but were made for collection and display, rather than for pasting up on city walls. David Blair screenprinted posters for about fifteen of the artists in his studio (the other artists had their own studios). The exhibition was a success, raising about NZ$6000 (personal communication with artist, 2022).Renewed protest activity in 1985 demonstrated that the same issues remained. The proposed tour was cancelled as a result of a successful legal challenge.

creator: Coalition Against Nuclear Warships

New Zealand University Students' Association
results.description:
This poster protested against the visit of the USS Truxtun to Wellington in 1982. The ship had visited previously in 1976 and 1980, and each visit had caused much protest in the ports of Wellington and Auckland because the USS Truxtun was designated as a 'Nuclear Guided Missile Cruiser'.
Nuclear ship visits
In 1971, the New Zealand government told the United States it would not accept visits by nuclear-powered vessels until the US accepted liability in the event of an accident. The US agreed to this in 1974. In 1976, the new government changed the policy to allow nuclear-capable warships to visit New Zealand ports. These visits were met with flotillas of protest yachts and boats.
Dangerous visitors
Anti-nuclear protest in New Zealand was distinctive because of these regular port visits. Though never used for nuclear testing, New Zealand was visited by about 120 American and British nuclear-powered or nuclear-armed vessels between 1960 and 1984. Since 1984, the New Zealand government has refused entry to all such vessels.

HART (Halt All Racist Tours)
results.description:
This poster was created for protests against the 1981 tour of New Zealand by the South African Springbok rugby team. Many New Zealanders objected to the tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid.
The poster called for a nationwide mobilisation on 1 May 1981 in an effort to force the New Zealand government to reconsider the tour. The poster features a crowd of black South Africans with their arms raised in the clenched-fist salute. The image of a protesting crowd is important to protest propaganda as it shows solidarity with a cause.
Thousands of people marched throughout the country on 1 May and on a second mobilisation on 3 July 1981. The tour went ahead, but protest action continued throughout, sometimes resulting in violence between protesters, supporters and police, eventually forcing the cancellation of two games.
Wellington Media Collective
The poster was designed and printed by Dave Kent and Chris Lipscombe of Wellington Media Collective. WMC was established in November 1978. Its mission statement 'We will work with you, not for you' enabled communities and activists to create advertising and protest material with the support of professional designers.

results.description:
This striking poster was made for the anti-Springbok Rugby Tour protest movement in 1981. It repurposes 'Apartheid' as 'Apart Hate', and includes an image of a policeman raising his baton to strike unarmed people. This is a detail from the famous photograph of a women’s protest at Cato Manor, Durban, in 1959, in which South African police subdued protesters with batons. This image of state oppression was incorporated into protest objects for many years afterwards, including t-shirts and posters.
Even though the image refers to police brutality in South Africa under the apartheid regime, it could also refer to the confrontations between rugby supporters, anti-tour protesters and police in New Zealand which grew increasingly violent as the tour in 1981 progressed. Police were equipped with long batons, helmets, and riot shields, and charged with ensuring that the games went ahead.
This particular poster belonged to activist Rona Bailey (1914-2005) who first became involved in protests against apartheid in South Africa from the late 1940s, and campaigned against the 1960 All Black tour of South Africa. For most of the 1970s, Bailey worked full-time and voluntarily for the anti-apartheid movement. Te Papa holds her hard hat worn during Springbok rugby tour protests in 1981 (GH011699).

results.description:
This poster protests against the South African government’s ‘honorary whites’ policy which enabled All Black Bryan Williams to tour South Africa with the All Blacks in the 1970s. Williams (born 1950, New Zealand) is of Samoan descent.
Until the All Black tour of South Africa in 1970, the New Zealand Rugby Union had bowed to South Africa’s apartheid laws and racist policies by sending the All Blacks without Māori and Pacific players, regardless of mounting protest pressure from many New Zealanders.
Background
Protests were voiced from the very first meeting of the South African and New Zealand rugby teams in 1921 when the Springboks visited New Zealand. When the Springboks played the New Zealand Māori team, a South African journalist's racist report published in South Africa was re-published in New Zealand papers, insulting Māori and supporters.
When the All Blacks made their first tour of South Africa in 1928, Māori players were not included. When the Springboks returned to New Zealand in 1937, Arawa iwi sought a social and sporting boycott of the tour. In 1949, despite protests, Māori players were not considered for the tour of South Africa. 
However, it wasn’t until the proposed 1960 All Black tour of South Africa that a wider protest movement arose (called the ‘No Maoris No Tour’). Two years of protests – including a massive petition, lobbying of government and direct action in the streets – brought the issue before all New Zealanders, but did not prevent the tour from going ahead.
In 1970 and 1976 protest demonstrations continued to play out in the streets as the All Blacks left to tour South Africa.
Sir Bryan Williams
Bryan Williams was only 19 when he debuted with the All Blacks and travelled to South Africa on the 1970 tour. He was the first Pacific player to represent New Zealand in rugby (three Māori players also went - they were all treated as 'honourary whites'). He went again to South Africa with the All Blacks in 1976 (five Māori players were included - again all were considered 'honourary whites').
After his playing career, Williams went on to coach Samoa. In 2018 Williams received a knighthood for his services to rugby and was inducted into World Rugby’s Hall of Fame.
In a 2018 interview with Rugby Pass, Williams commented on his participation in the 1970 tour to South Africa. He considered himself to be socially engaged as a law student, and personally believed he was making a genuine stand against apartheid. Reflecting on his involvement: ‘…I guess it was only in later life that you realise the significance of it. It just created a small dent in the armor of apartheid that they were willing to accept four of us as the first coloured players to go to South Africa, and that had some impact down the line’ (https://www.rugbypass.com/news/in-conversation-with-sir-bryan-williams/).
Rona Bailey
This particular poster belonged to activist Rona Bailey (1914-2005) who first became involved in protests against apartheid in South Africa from the late 1940s, and campaigned against the 1960 All Black tour of South Africa. For most of the 1970s, Bailey worked full-time and voluntarily for the anti-apartheid movement. Te Papa holds her hard hat worn during Springbok rugby tour protests in 1981 (GH011699).

results.description:
This original artwork was created for a poster to advertise a protest against the 1981 tour of New Zealand by the South African Springbok rugby team. Many New Zealanders objected to the tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid.
The poster called for a nationwide mobilisation on 1 May 1981 in an effort to force the New Zealand government to reconsider the tour. The tour went ahead, but protest action continued throughout, sometimes resulting in violence between protesters, supporters and police, eventually forcing the cancellation of two games.
The artwork combines crowd scenes from two different photographs - one of black South African children (in the background) and one of New Zealand protesters (in the foreground).
